title: Searching for the ox
hookLine: picture one: the herder searches, not knowing what he's lost (Ox-Herding 1)
tomorrow: why would a Zen picture send the herder to the books?

cards: Open the fridge, stand there, forget what you came for: Kuoan's first picture is that moment, stretched across a whole landscape. A herder stands alone in tall grass, pushing it aside with both hands.

In the verse Kuoan, a Chinese Zen teacher, wrote beside it, the rivers are wide, the mountains far, and the path keeps going. He's worn out. Evening comes, and all he hears is cicadas in the maple trees.
He's looking for his ox, and he couldn't tell you where he lost it.

teach.b: Here's the strange part. The short preface to this picture says the ox was never lost. So why search?

teach.h: HE TURNED HIS BACK ON HIMSELF.
teach.b: Because, it says, the herder turned his back on himself, and the ox wandered off into the dust. Home looks farther away every day.
He stands at crossroads, unsure which way to go, burning with wanting to gain and fearing to lose. Notice what's missing from that list: a map. He isn't searching because he's clever.
He's searching because something in him won't settle.
That's the teaching, and it's Zen's own: what you're looking for is your own true nature, what Zen teachers call Buddha-nature, and it was never somewhere else. The search doesn't make it.
The search begins because you looked away. And Kuoan doesn't mock the herder.
He makes the searching itself the first picture of the way, drawn with the same care as the last.

Tired, a little lost, hearing cicadas: that's where the path starts, even while the searcher thinks he's nowhere. This path started the same way, with one breath at the bottom of a hill and no idea what the climb was for.
One to tell a friend tonight: the ox in these pictures isn't a prize you win. It stands for the very self that's doing the looking.

how: Zen students read Kuoan's ten ox-herding pictures, each with a short preface and verse, as a map of practice. People on this path look back at why they began.

games.q: what does “searching for the ox” mean?
o: a Chinese tale of a stolen ox and a village trial
a farm chore Zen monks did each morning at dawn
the first picture: looking for what was never lost

p: where he stands, unsure of the way

s: in Kuoan's first picture, the herder knows exactly where the ox went
he's searching and can't say where he lost it; the rivers are wide and the path goes on.
The preface says the ox was never really lost
the herder turned his back on himself, so the ox wandered into the dust.
the ox in the pictures is a prize you earn by practicing hard
the popular reading. it stands for your own true nature, already there.

games.q: a friend says she's not 'spiritual enough' to start, because she doesn't even know what she's looking for. what fits Kuoan's first picture?
o: start anyway: the first picture is someone searching who doesn't know yet.
wait until she knows exactly what she wants out of it first.
searching means something is missing in her that practice must add.
games.why: Kuoan's first picture is a herder who doesn't know where the ox is. the preface says the ox was never lost: the searching is already the first step of the way.

practice: Find any scrap of paper and write one line by hand: why you began this, back at the bottom of the hill, in whatever words come. Then sit with it for the two minutes, the way the herder stands in the grass, not knowing yet.

wordCard.voice: Searching for the ox: Kuoan's first picture, a herder alone in the grass, looking for what was never lost.

orig.note: Chinese: searching for the ox, the title of Kuoan's first picture.

carryVoice: Keep this one: searching, the picture Kuoan drew first, before any ox appears. Day three of the summit, done.
